title: Warehouse Bin Grid
story: A parts warehouse stores bins on a wall of shelves. Each bin has a code. The codes grow from left to right along a shelf, and each shelf starts with a code larger than the last code on the shelf above it. Some codes were retired, so the numbers skip.
A picker gets an order for a code and wants to know, before climbing a ladder, whether that bin exists anywhere on the wall.
task: Write hasBin(grid, code). grid[r][c] is the code on shelf r, position c. Every shelf has the same number of bins. Reading the shelves top to bottom, each left to right, gives one strictly increasing sequence.
Return true if code is in the grid, otherwise false. An empty grid (no shelves) returns false. Aim for O(log(rows × cols)).
constraints: Read row by row, the codes are strictly increasing.

examples.explanation: Laid end to end, the 12 codes form one sorted line. 142 is at position 6 of that line, which is shelf 1, slot 2.
125 would sit between 121 (end of shelf 0) and 130 (start of shelf 1). Neither is 125, and nothing else can be, so the bin does not exist.

hints: Imagine unbolting the shelves and placing them end to end in one long row. Is that row sorted?
It is: 103, 108, 115, 121, 130, 134, … So this is ordinary binary search on a list of rows × cols items. The only question is how to read item number p without building the list.
With 4 bins per shelf, item 6 of the long row is on shelf 1 (6 ÷ 4, rounded down) at slot 2 (the remainder). How does that generalise?
Binary search over positions 0 to rows × cols - 1. For a middle position p, read grid[floor(p / cols)][p % cols] and compare with code as usual.
bruteForce: Check every bin, shelf by shelf. That is O(rows × cols): 40,000 bins for a 200 × 200 wall.

A middle ground is to binary search each shelf separately, O(rows × log cols). Better, but it still ignores that the shelves are sorted against each other. One binary search over the whole wall needs about 16 looks.

py: def has_bin(grid: list[list[int]], code: int) -> bool:

tests.note: in the gap between two rows

js: let lo = 0, hi = grid.length * cols - 1; // positions in the long row
py: lo, hi = 0, len(grid) * cols - 1  # positions in the long row
walkthrough: The grid is just a sorted list folded into rows. Search it as one list, and convert a position to a shelf and slot only when you need to read a value: shelf = floor(p / cols), slot = p % cols.
Trace the 3 × 4 example looking for 142. Positions run from 0 to 11:

A common slip is dividing by the number of rows instead of the number of columns. The column count is how many positions each shelf uses up, so it is what you divide by. The single-column and single-row tests catch the mix-up.
solution.timeWhy: One binary search over all rows × cols positions.
solution.spaceWhy: No flattened copy is built; positions are converted on the fly.
solution.takeaway: If a 2D grid is sorted when read row by row, treat it as one virtual sorted list and map position p to row p / cols, column p % cols. Index arithmetic often saves you from building a copy.
